newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Ross and Arafat start talks on Middle East crisis.
newsitem.headline: Ross and Arafat start talks on Middle East crisis.

text.p: U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross began talks on Thursday with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on a brewing crisis over Jewish settlements in Jerusalem and Palestinian-Israeli violence which are threatening peace.

Ross made no comment on arrival at a villa in the Moroccan capital. But Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa and Arafat told reporters shortly before Ross arrived that their talks were focused on Jerusalem.
Moussa said he has met the Saudi, Syrian and Gulf foreign ministers, who are in Rabat for a meeting of the Jerusalem Committee and have briefed Arafat on their views.
Their views, he said, were unanimous.
"The issue of Jerusalem is sensitive. We cannot accept this way of dealing with the issue of Jerusalem, dealing with us as Arabs, with the conventions and the law covering this situation."
Arafat described the Israeli construction of settlements in the East Jerusalem hilltop which the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and the Israelis call Har Homa as "a crime".

Ross, who arrived in Rabat on Wednesday evening, was sent by U.S. President Bill Clinton with messages to Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to try to stop Israeli-Palestinian violence and restart peace talks.

"There is a message with Dennis Ross from President Clinton... We shall see," Arafat told reporters on arrival at Rabat airport. Ross was due to leave Morocco for Israel later on Thursday where he would hold similar talks with Netanyahu.

Israel's groundbreaking on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem has ignited eight days of violence including clashes between Israeli troops and Palestinian stone-throwers and the killing of three Israeli women last Friday by a Palestinian suicide bomber who blew himself up at a Tel Aviv cafe.
Ross said he would return to Washington by the weekend to report to Clinton on his discussions so the "president can decide what the next proper move should be".
Palestinian officials have urged Ross to lean on Israel to halt work on the East Jerusalem hilltop.
The Israeli housing project enraged Palestinians who regard East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War, as the future capital of an independent Palestinian state.

Fifteen foreign ministers of Islamic countries were in Rabat for the Jerusalem Committee meeting, which was called by King Hassan of Morocco to discuss ways to counter Israel's latest housing project.
The Jerusalem Committee, headed by the king, was set up by an Islamic Conference Organisation summit in 1975 with the aim of preventing Israel from making any demographic changes to Jerusalem.
